clue.text: Part of fish, large on threshing shark

indicators.note: threshing beats grain about, so the word before it is knocked into a new order

blocks.note: a fin is one part of a fish
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A fisherman describes a piece of a big fish lying on the deck while it is threshed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the fish part sits on top of the reworked letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A shark in the sense of a swindler or cheat is someone who uses trickery, which is exactly what a finagler does.

clue.text: Mark eyed in first year

indicators.note: something eyed within a phrase is spotted inside it, lurking across the word boundary

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark was spotted during his first year at school or college.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a boy's name but it is the definition, and 'eyed' neatly hints at where this blemish appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is a small red swelling on the eyelid, a visible blemish or spot on the face.

clue.text: Seller of food that's less appetising, we hear?

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken form, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: grosser means more disgusting, so less appetising

explanation.surface: A sly dig at a shopkeeper whose produce is unappealing.
explanation.definitionFit: A grocer runs a shop selling food and household provisions to the public.

clue.text: See 10 Across
22 down character personifies a despicable pleb loather

indicators.note: something despicable is twisted and corrupt, so the following words are bent out of shape

blocks.note: to personify something is to be it in human form
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A snobbish character in a novel embodies contempt for the common people.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 down is Austen; this mercenary flirt appears in Northanger Abbey. A pleb is a common person.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella Thorpe is the scheming friend of the heroine Catherine Morland in Jane Austen's novel Northanger Abbey.

clue.text: For example, Fitzgerald's behind sacrifice, 22 down character

blocks.note: Fitzgerald is an example of an American writer, and an American's word for the behind is this
the price of something is what must be given up for it

explanation.surface: A note on what the Great Gatsby author gave up for literature, or his backside.
explanation.walkthrough: F Scott Fitzgerald was American, and in American English fanny means the bottom; in Britain the word is far ruder.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Price is the modest heroine of Jane Austen's novel Mansfield Park, the 22 down author.

clue.text: 22 down's Mr. Collins, say, cut from poem and caught

indicators.note: taking one thing from another removes it, leaving the remainder behind

blocks.note: a comic four-line biographical verse form
to hew is to cut with an axe
cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Austen's pompous clergyman is chopped out of a poem and arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like the deletion signal but it supplies the letters removed; 'from' tells you to take them away.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Collins in Pride and Prejudice is a clergyman, and a cleric is any member of the clergy, so he is an example.

clue.text: Arguably an excess of emotion when cataloguing bug?

definitions.text: Arguably an excess of emotion when cataloguing bug?

blocks.clueFragment: Arguably an excess of emotion when cataloguing
blocks.note: surface: a fit of nerves or frenzy brought on by compiling lists
setter's reading: a bacterium whose name sounds like hysteria with the word for a catalogue in front

explanation.surface: Someone gets overwrought from making too many lists.
explanation.walkthrough: Hysteria is an excess of emotion; make its start a list and you have the food-poisoning germ. 'Arguably' admits the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Listeria is a bacterium that causes food poisoning, and bug is everyday slang for any germ.

clue.text: Stop and stand

blocks.note: first meaning: to come to a halt, as an engine does
second meaning: a booth or table selling goods at a market

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an instruction to halt and stay upright, but the second word is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to cease moving when an engine cuts out and a trader's booth at a market.

clue.text: Beautiful message by 22 down – for her character

blocks.note: the first name of the author at 22 down
fair is an old word for beautiful
a document sent by telephone line

explanation.surface: An admiring note is sent by a famous novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By 22 down' seems to mean written by her, but it places her first name beside the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Fairfax is the accomplished young woman in Austen's novel Emma, so she is one of that author's creations.

clue.text: Roman copper coin, a rare fake featuring head of Balbinus

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the opening letter of the name is used
a fake is a counterfeit, so the words are forged into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
Balbinus was a third-century Roman emperor

explanation.surface: A collector describes a counterfeit rare Roman copper coin bearing an emperor's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman copper coin' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'copper', meaning police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is slang for a police officer, and this is a member of an armed police corps such as Italy's.

clue.text: 22 down character remains attached to English lord in senselessly joining club

indicators.note: read as sense-less, meaning the word sense is dropped from the phrase it follows
one piece is placed within another, so the remainder sits inside the noble
joining means connecting the final piece onto the end of the others

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for English
taken as written
what survives of the phrase in sense once that noun goes
ash is what remains after burning
a wood is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: An aristocrat joins a club for no good reason, leaving his remains behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke: this heroine stands for Sense in Sense and Sensibility, and the clue removes sense. 'In' does double duty as letters and placement.
explanation.definitionFit: Elinor Dashwood is the sensible elder sister in Jane Austen's novel Sense and Sensibility.

clue.text: Book contains three-fifths of tales untold

indicators.note: the following word has five letters, so this keeps just three of them, the closing trio
to contain is to hold inside, so the book wraps around the kept letters

blocks.note: Numbers is the fourth book of the Old Testament
the last three of its five letters

explanation.surface: A volume holds a selection of stories that have never been told.
explanation.walkthrough: Book is a Bible book here; the kept letters go just before its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Untold can mean too many to count, which is what numberless means: innumerable, beyond reckoning.

clue.text: Game pie calls for dried fruit

indicators.note: game here is an adjective meaning willing or up for anything, so the letters are ready to be played with

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A game pie recipe requires some dried fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game pie' reads as a pheasant or venison pie; game is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Allspice is the dried unripe berry of the pimento tree, used whole or ground as a spice.

clue.text: Comedic theatre where amusing hosts made merry

indicators.note: merry means tipsy, so the word before it reels into a new order
a host holds guests within, so the outer word takes the other letters inside

blocks.note: dry humour is understated and amusing
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A funny play whose hosts made everyone merry.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters go between the R and Y of the wit word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramedy is a television or stage genre blending drama and comedy, so comic theatre of a kind.

clue.text: See 12 Across
Foot carrying cut, very anxious

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so the outer word holds the other inside

blocks.note: to foot the bill is to pay it
a nick is a small cut

explanation.surface: Someone carrying a cut on their foot is understandably worried.
explanation.walkthrough: Foot looks like a body part but is the verb meaning to settle a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone panicky is gripped by sudden fear and alarm, extremely nervous.

clue.text: In speech, 22 down character's noble

indicators.note: speech is spoken, so a name is matched to a word by sound alone

blocks.note: Mr Knightley is the hero of Austen's Emma

explanation.surface: A claim that a novelist's character is spoken of as dignified.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname has an extra E; said out loud it matches the adjective exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Knightly means befitting a knight: chivalrous, honourable and gallant, hence noble in conduct.

clue.text: Bad day punctuating a creative work

indicators.note: punctuating means breaking into something at intervals, so one piece is inserted within another

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for day
poetry is a creative work

explanation.surface: A poor day interrupts someone's artistic project.
explanation.walkthrough: The day letter goes between the A and the poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse means harmful or unfavourable, as in adverse weather, a formal synonym of bad.

clue.text: On the rack – in italics?

blocks.note: first meaning: under great strain, tormented as on the torture instrument
second meaning: emphasised, as type is when slanted; the first phrase is itself printed slanted

explanation.walkthrough: The clue's opening words are set in italics, so they are literally emphasised as well as meaning under pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both under pressure or anxious and given emphasis, as italic type gives words in printing.

clue.text: See 5
One that's correct, though not entirely sharp

indicators.note: something not entirely there is incomplete, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
a tick marks an answer as correct

explanation.surface: Someone who is right but not altogether clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp' looks like 'clever' but means sour, as in taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetic means like vinegar, containing acetic acid, so it has a sour, sharp taste.

clue.text: Author, 'X' from Oz?

blocks.note: abbreviation for Australia, nicknamed Oz
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A writer is known by a mere X, as if signing from the Wizard's land.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is a nickname for Australia, not the Wizard's kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen was the English novelist who wrote Pride and Prejudice, Emma and other classic novels.

clue.text: LS's extra dining room?

blocks.note: setter's reading: the two letters are what remains of a four-letter word for limbs once its middle is emptied
surface reading: a spare room for eating in; the idiom is about someone able to eat endlessly

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is joked about as limbs emptied out (leaving only their outer letters) and as a capacity for eating any amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone said to have this can consume huge amounts of food or drink without visible effect, as if storing the excess.

clue.text: Drunkard, sweating, dropping time and time again in London area

indicators.note: dropping means letting something fall away, so the named letter is removed from each word

blocks.note: a sot is a habitual drinker
someone sweating is hot
T is the abbreviation for time, taken once and then again

explanation.surface: A perspiring drunk staggers about a London district, losing time repeatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: One T goes from each of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is a district of London's West End famous for nightlife, restaurants and theatres.

clue.text: Long narrative, a talk written up

indicators.note: in a down clue, writing upwards means the letters run from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
gas is idle chatter

explanation.surface: A lengthy story or a lecture is written down.
explanation.walkthrough: To gas is to chatter, so talk gives the three-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long story of heroic deeds, originally Norse or Icelandic, or any lengthy tale.

clue.text: Greenfly for example with love for green stuff

blocks.note: greenfly is an aphid, a garden pest
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A gardener's view of aphids and fondness for greenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Pesto is a green Italian sauce of basil, pine nuts, garlic, cheese and olive oil.

clue.text: Mesmerising guru, one accompanying Scandinavian lass

blocks.note: a typical Scandinavian man's name
gal is an informal word for a girl
Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A hypnotic guru travels with a Nordic girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accompanying' puts the one after the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali is the hypnotist in du Maurier's novel Trilby, now a name for anyone exerting controlling influence.
